title: Most harm we do ourselves
hook: he argues most suffering comes from what people do to themselves and each other

segments.voice: Yesterday, the leaf, the palace, and care that follows the mind. Your line: providence follows attention. Today, suffering, sorted.

A writer once argued that the world holds more evil than good. Count up the pain, the sickness, the grief, he said, and the scale tips the wrong way. Maimonides answered it in the Guide. He didn't deny that suffering is real. He did something more uncomfortable. He sorted it, kind by kind, and asked where it actually comes from. And when the sorting was done, the biggest pile wasn't the one blamed on God or on nature.
screen: `MORE EVIL THAN GOOD?` → `SORT THE SUFFERING.` → `WHICH PILE IS BIGGEST?`

segments.voice: Most harm we do ourselves. From the Guide, part three, chapter twelve. First, the harm of having a body. Bodies come into being and wear out: illness, injury, the blows of nature. Real, Maimonides says, but the least frequent. Second, the harm people do to each other: tyranny, violence, war. More common than the first, but still not the largest. Third, the harm people do to themselves. This, he says, is the most frequent of all. Too much eating, too much drinking, appetites without limits, chasing more than anyone needs. A person wrecks their health, their peace, their relationships, and then complains about the world. Some readers find in his discussion that the hunger for luxuries also turns people against each other, so the third kind feeds the second. He quotes Ecclesiastes: "God made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions." Fourth, why the writer got it wrong. A person who thinks the whole universe exists for them judges everything by their own small hurts, and so concludes the world is mostly bad. Step back, and much of what we suffer turns out to be within reach of human choice. This is not a teaching that blames people for their illnesses or their grief. Maimonides keeps the first kind on the list. It hands back some power: the largest pile is one people can begin to shrink.
screen: `THE BODY WEARS OUT.` · `WHAT PEOPLE DO TO EACH OTHER.` · `WHAT PEOPLE DO TO THEMSELVES.` · `THE WORLD IS NOT ABOUT ME.` · then, large: `MOST HARM WE DO OURSELVES.`

segments.voice: Think back over the past week to one thing that went wrong, and sort it gently, the way Maimonides would: the body or nature simply happening, something another person did, or some small part that was yours, a habit, an excess, a word. Don't punish yourself; just find the part that's yours, and one step that would care for it. If what hurts ever feels like too much to carry, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

Most harm we do ourselves. Maimonides' teaching that of the three kinds of suffering, the most frequent is what people bring on themselves, and much of the rest is what they do to each other. Today's word.
screen: `MOST HARM WE DO OURSELVES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: most harm we do. Held gently, that's hopeful: much of it is within reach. Go gently.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching on repentance asks a person to examine their own part in what went wrong, and some study Maimonides' account of the three kinds of evil in Guide 3:12 alongside his Laws of Repentance.
